title: Infra Team Playbook: GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts, IaC, CI/CD, and Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates infrastructure engineering best practices used by the eng-infra team: GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, runbooks for day-2 operations, and guidance for maintaining the infra team wiki. It is intended for engineers onboarding to infra, on-call SREs, and platform owners.

Scope and audience

- Scope: global GPU fleet (hosted + Dedicated), cloud accounts (AWS primary, GCP for backups), networking, core Terraform modules, Buildkite CI/CD pipelines, and operational runbooks.
- Audience: infra engineers, SREs, platform/product owners, and security reviewers.

Owner & contacts

- Primary owner: eng-infra team (pager: eng-infra-oncall rotation)
- Doc owner: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.example.com)
- Pager rotations: see team wiki rota page (link internal)

High-level architecture

- GPU fleet: managed pools per deployment mode (hosted/dedicated/private). Pool manager service: infra-gpu-orchestrator (K8s controller).
- Control plane: infra-control (private control plane for Private deployments).
- IaC: Terraform modules in git repo infra/terraform-modules (monorepo), module registry via internal registry.
- CI/CD: Buildkite for infra pipelines, GitHub for PRs and branch protection.

GPU fleet and capacity planning

Goals and SLOs

| Item | Target |
|------|--------|
| GPU utilization (avg across cluster) | 60% - 75% |
| Queue length (requests waiting for a GPU) | < 10 sustained for 5m |
| Scale-up reaction time | <= 3 minutes (target) |
| Emergency reserve capacity | 10% of committed pool |
| Cost-efficiency target | Cost per generated token within benchmarked profile +/- 15% |

Key instance types (AWS examples)

- p4d.24xlarge (A100) - high throughput training/large batch workloads
- g5.48xlarge (H100) - low latency inference and optimal perf for 8k context
- g5.12xlarge / a10g - smaller inference / canary and burst pools

Autoscaling policy (recommended)

1. Metrics used: queued_requests (per-pool), avg_gpu_utilization(1m), total_active_models, pod_start_success_rate.
2. Scale-up triggers (OR):
   - queued_requests > 20 for 2m OR
   - avg_gpu_utilization > 80% for 5m OR
   - scheduled capacity window requires > 90% of committed capacity.
3. Scale-down policy: reduce by 1 instance at a time if avg_gpu_utilization < 50% for 10m and queued_requests == 0.
4. Minimum pool size: defined per pool (example: hosted-default min=2, dedicated-min=2, private-min=1).

Capacity planning formula (simple)

Estimated GPUs required = ceil((QPS * avg_tokens_per_request * avg_inference_time_per_token_ms) / (tokens_per_second_per_gpu * 1000) ) + buffer

Example: QPS=50, avg_tokens=200, avg_time_per_token=5ms, gpu_tps=500 =>
N = ceil((50*200*5) / (500*1000)) + 0.1*calc ~ ceil(50000/500000) + small => 1 GPU + buffer => provision 2 GPUs

Cloud accounts and networking

Account model and ownership

- Management account: redwood-root (billing and org-wide policies)
- Production account(s): prod-us-east-1, prod-eu-west-1 (owned by eng-infra)
- Non-prod accounts: staging, dev, bench (owned by platform teams)
- Dedicated customer accounts: per-customer AWS accounts for Dedicated/Private deployments (managed via infra/account-manager).

Networking patterns

- VPC layout: per-account VPCs with 3 AZ subnets (public/private/management).
- CIDR allocation: use alloc blocks from central CIDR pool (see CIDR registry page).
- Peering & Transit: use Transit Gateway for production interconnects; VPC Peering only for short-lived test networks.
- Egress: NAT Gateway in each AZ; central egress endpoints for common SaaS providers via proxy.

IAM & security best practices

- Principle of least privilege: Terraform-managed IAM roles, short-lived credentials for CI/CD, and OIDC-based GitHub Actions/Buildkite agents.
- Cross-account roles: assume-role pattern for deployments from pipeline account to prod accounts.
- Key management: use KMS aliases per account and HSM for sensitive customer keys in Private deployments.

Terraform / IaC modules and conventions

Repository layout (convention)

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| infra/terraform-modules/networking | VPC / subnet / TGW modules |
| infra/terraform-modules/gpu | GPU pool, autoscaler, launch templates |
| infra/terraform-modules/iam | Common IAM role and policy templates |
| infra/environments/prod-us-east-1 | Live TF configs for prod account |

Module naming and versioning

- Module names: <service>-<component>-module (e.g., gpu-pool-module).
- Release: tag modules with semver. Use automated CI to publish to internal module registry.

Example usage (terraform snippet)

```hcl
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra.git//terraform-modules/gpu?ref=v1.3.0"
  name   = "hosted-default"
  min_size = 2
  max_size = 40
  instance_type = "g5.48xlarge"
  scale_policy = {
    scale_up_threshold = 0.80
    scale_down_threshold = 0.50
  }
}
```

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipelines and responsibilities

- infra/ci/plan-and-apply: Buildkite pipeline for Terraform plan and apply. Tagged with protected branches.
- infra/ci/modules-test: Unit + integration tests for modules, runs on PR.
- infra/ci/gpu-canary: Canary deployment pipeline for GPU pool changes (requires manual approval).

Branching and promotion flow

1. All changes must be made in feature branches and go through PR review.
2. Module changes -> merge to main -> modules-test -> publish module artifact.
3. Environment changes (prod) -> PR to env branch with terraform plan produced by CI -> requires two approvers + oncall sign-off for infra-impacting changes.

Buildkite pipeline example (excerpt)

```yaml
steps:
  - label: ":terraform: plan"
    command: "scripts/terraform_plan.sh $BUILDKITE_BRANCH"
    agents:
      queue: infra
    env:
      TF_LOG: info
  - wait
  - label: ":terraform: apply"
    command: "scripts/terraform_apply.sh $BUILDKITE_BRANCH"
    if: "build.pull_request == false && build.branch == \"main\""
    agents:
      queue: infra
    concurrency: 1
    soft_fail: false
```

Artifact and state management

- Remote state: S3 with DynamoDB locking (prod and staging). Terraform state encryption enabled via KMS.
- State access: limited to CI service role and designated engineers via cross-account assume-role.

Testing and validation

- Unit tests: terratest where feasible.
- Integration: smoke deploy on a test account, validate health checks and GPU node readiness.
- Security scan: run tfsec and checkov in CI.

Infra runbooks and operational playbooks

Runbook index (must be kept up-to-date):

1. gpu-pool-scale-up-playbook - steps to manually add capacity and warm nodes
2. gpu-node-failure - triage failed instance replacement and eviction recovery
3. terraform-apply-failures - roll-forward/rollback guidance for failed applies
4. network-outage - failover steps for transit gateway and route table reconciliation

Example runbook: gpu-pool-scale-up-playbook

Purpose: Add emergency capacity to a GPU pool if autoscaler is lagging.

Steps:
1. Check metrics: Grafana dashboard infra/gpu-fleet -> queued_requests, gpu_util, pod_start_time.
2. Confirm quota: aws service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code ec2 --region us-east-1 | grep GPU
3. Manually increase ASG desired count:
   - CLI (for ASG-backed pools): aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name hosted-default-asg --desired-capacity 5 --region us-east-1
   - For K8s nodepool (EKS): eksctl scale nodegroup --cluster prod-cluster --name gpu-nodegroup --nodes 5
4. Warm nodes: run health check job: kubectl apply -f infra/k8s/warmup-job.yaml -n infra-system
5. Verify: Grafana shows avg_gpu_utilization drop below threshold and queued_requests decreases.
6. Post-incident: open incident ticket, record root cause, update runbook if steps blocked.

Incident triage checklist (short)

- Severity assessment: Determine P0 vs P1 (P0 = production impact > 50% requests failing or latency SLO broken)
- Pager and owners: alert-eng-infra -> oncall -> rotate if needed
- Collect evidence: logs (CloudWatch), metrics (Prometheus), recent deploys (CI build id), terraform changes in last 24h.
- Mitigation: rollback or add capacity depending on failure mode.
- RCA: within 72 hours, postmortem and corrective actions.

Maintenance windows and change control

- Regular maintenance windows: Tue/Wed 02:00-04:00 UTC for non-critical infra changes.
- Emergency changes: use emergency change channel and require approver + oncall.

Observability and dashboards

- Dashboards: infra/gpu-fleet, infra/terraform-ops, infra-network-overview. Important panels: queued requests (per pool), pod_start_latency (p95), gpu_utilization (p95), ASG desired vs actual.
- Alerts: Pager thresholds: queued_requests > 50 for 3m -> P1; pod_start_failure_rate > 5% for 5m -> P1; avg_gpu_utilization > 90% for 5m -> P1

Documentation & team wiki hygiene

- Page structure: use confluence headings, short intro, contact and owner fields, step-by-step procedures, and related pages.
- Keep runbooks small: single-purpose pages with links to deeper docs.
- Review cadence: owners must review critical runbooks quarterly.

Appendix: useful CLI snippets and snippets repo

- List GPU nodes: kubectl get nodes -l gpu=true -o wide
- Describe failing pod: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace>
- Terraform plan for prod: scripts/terraform_plan.sh prod-us-east-1
- Quick check service quotas: aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-XXXXXXXX

Contact and escalation

- Pager: #pager-eng-infra on Slack (alerting integrates with Opsgenie)
- On-call rotation: documented in team wiki rota page (link)
- Escalation: oncall -> infra lead -> eng director (if incident > 4 hours or cross-account exposure)
